subject: Physics
question: The equation of a progressive wave is y = 0.05 sin(200 π t - π x), where all quantities are in SI units. The speed of the wave is:
explanation: Comparing with y = A sin(ω t - k x) gives ω = 200 π rad s⁻¹ and k = π rad m⁻¹. Hence v = ω/k = 200 π/π = 200 m s⁻¹. As a check, f = ω/2 π = 100 Hz and λ = 2 π/k = 2 m, so v = 100 × 2 = 200 m s⁻¹.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The wave described by y = A sin(ω t - k x) travels:

options.A: nowhere, since the equation represents a stationary wave

explanation: Keeping the phase constant, ω t - k x = constant, so x = (ω/k) t + constant. As time increases, x increases, so the wave advances along the positive x direction.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: For a distinct echo to be heard, the reflecting surface must be:

options.A: polished to a mirror finish, since only optically smooth surfaces can reflect waves
options.B: large compared with the wavelength of the sound and far enough away for the reflected sound to arrive after the direct sound has ceased to be sensed
options.C: made of a soft absorbing material such as cloth, which returns the sound most efficiently
options.D: small compared with the wavelength of the sound, so that the sound is reflected from a sharp point

correct_answer: large compared with the wavelength of the sound and far enough away for the reflected sound to arrive after the direct sound has ceased to be sensed
explanation: Two conditions must be met. Geometrically, the reflector must be large compared with the wavelength, otherwise the sound bends around it. In time, the echo must arrive at least about 0.1 s after the direct sound, which for air at 340 m s⁻¹ places the reflector at least 17 m away. A hard dense surface reflects far better than a soft porous one.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A compression pulse travelling along the air in a tube reaches the open end of the tube. The pulse reflected back into the tube is:

options.A: a compression of half the original amplitude, since only half the energy is returned
options.B: a compression, since the sign of the pressure change is preserved at every kind of boundary
options.C: neither a compression nor a rarefaction, since no reflection occurs at an open end
options.D: a rarefaction, since a compression arriving at a free boundary is returned with the sign of the pressure change reversed

correct_answer: a rarefaction, since a compression arriving at a free boundary is returned with the sign of the pressure change reversed
explanation: At the open end the air is free to move outward into the large body of atmosphere, so the excess pressure there must fall to the ambient value. The reflected pulse must therefore cancel the incident excess pressure at that point, which requires it to be a rarefaction. The displacement, in contrast, suffers no reversal at a free boundary. This is the exact opposite of what happens at a rigid wall.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A student stands 165 m from a wall, claps, and finds that the echo returns after 1 s. From this measurement the speed of sound in the air is:
explanation: The sound covers 165 m to the wall and 165 m back, a total of 330 m, in 1 s. Hence v = 330 / 1 = 330 m s⁻¹. This kind of open air measurement is the simplest classroom determination of the speed of sound.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A SONAR set works at a frequency of 50 kHz. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m s⁻¹ and the echo from the sea bed returns 2 s after the pulse is sent. The wavelength of the pulse in water and the depth of the sea are respectively:
explanation: The wavelength is λ = v / f = 1500 / 50000 = 0.03 m = 3 cm, short enough to give a well directed beam. The total path is v t = 1500 × 2 = 3000 m, so the depth is 3000 / 2 = 1500 m.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: When a sound wave is reflected from a large smooth wall,:

options.A: the frequency of the sound is halved on reflection while the direction obeys the law of reflection
options.B: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane
options.C: the angle of reflection is always zero, so that the sound returns straight back along the incident path
options.D: the angle of reflection equals twice the angle of incidence, because sound is a longitudinal wave

correct_answer: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane
explanation: Reflection is a general property of waves and does not depend on whether the wave is longitudinal or transverse. A sound wave striking a large rigid surface obeys exactly the same two laws as a light ray, and this is what makes sound reflectors, whispering galleries and megaphones work.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A wave of wavelength 0.6 m is reflected from a rigid boundary. The extra path difference that is equivalent to the phase change introduced by this reflection is:
explanation: Path difference and phase difference are related by path = (λ/2 π) x phase. For a phase change of π this gives (0.6/2 π) x π = 0.3 m, that is half a wavelength.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Consider the following two statements. Statement 1: at a free boundary the reflected transverse pulse is not inverted. Statement 2: at a free boundary the particle at the boundary has zero displacement. Which of the following is true?

options.A: Statement 1 and statement 2 are both correct
options.B: Statement 1 is incorrect and statement 2 is correct
options.C: Statement 1 and statement 2 are both incorrect
options.D: Statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is incorrect

correct_answer: Statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is incorrect
explanation: At a free end the boundary particle is unconstrained and is driven to twice the incident displacement, so it is an antinode and its displacement is certainly not zero. The uninverted reflection is exactly what makes this large displacement possible.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: When a wave is reflected from a free boundary, that is from a rarer medium, the reflected wave suffers:
explanation: At a free boundary the end is able to move and in fact reaches maximum displacement. Incident and reflected displacements must add there rather than cancel, which requires zero phase change.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: When a longitudinal sound wave is reflected from a rigid wall, the reflected wave shows:

options.A: a phase change of π in the displacement but no phase change in the pressure variation
options.B: a phase change of π in the pressure variation but none in the displacement
options.C: no phase change in either the displacement or the pressure variation
options.D: a phase change of π in both the displacement and the pressure variation

correct_answer: a phase change of π in the displacement but no phase change in the pressure variation
explanation: Zero net displacement at the wall requires the reflected displacement to be the negative of the incident displacement, a phase change of π. Pressure is related to the spatial gradient of displacement, so where displacement reverses the pressure does not, and the pressure variations add at the wall.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
subtopic: Reflection at the open end of a pipe
question: At the open end of an organ pipe, an incident compression is reflected as:

options.A: a compression, and the open end behaves as a displacement node
options.B: a compression, and the open end behaves as a displacement antinode
options.C: a rarefaction, and the open end behaves as a displacement node
options.D: a rarefaction, and the open end behaves as a displacement antinode

correct_answer: a rarefaction, and the open end behaves as a displacement antinode
explanation: At the open end the air is free to expand into the atmosphere, so the excess pressure there must stay close to zero. The reflected pressure wave is therefore inverted, and a compression returns as a rarefaction, while the displacement is unreversed and maximum, making the end an antinode.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A wave is reflected back into the same medium from which it came. Which quantities are altered by this reflection?

options.A: the wavelength changes while the frequency stays the same
options.B: the frequency, the wavelength and the speed all change
options.C: the speed changes while the frequency and the wavelength stay the same
options.D: only the direction of propagation and, at a rigid boundary, the phase

correct_answer: only the direction of propagation and, at a rigid boundary, the phase
explanation: The source continues to vibrate at the same rate, so the frequency of the reflected wave equals that of the incident wave. The medium is the same, so the speed is the same, and therefore λ = v/f is also the same. Only the direction reverses, together with a phase change of π if the boundary is rigid.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
subtopic: Pulse at a junction of two strings
question: A pulse travelling along a light string reaches a junction where the light string is joined to a much heavier string. Which statement describes what happens?

options.A: The reflected pulse is inverted, because the heavier string behaves as the denser and more rigid medium
options.B: The transmitted pulse is inverted while the reflected pulse remains erect
options.C: The reflected pulse is erect, because the junction is free to move
options.D: There is no reflected pulse at all, since the whole pulse is transmitted into the heavy string

correct_answer: The reflected pulse is inverted, because the heavier string behaves as the denser and more rigid medium
explanation: The wave speed on a string is √(T/m), so a heavier string carries the wave more slowly and acts as the denser medium. Reflection from a denser medium introduces a phase change of π, which appears as an inverted reflected pulse, while the pulse transmitted into the heavy string stays erect.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The displacement of a particle is x = 3 sin(π t) + 4 cos(π t) cm. The amplitude of the resulting SHM is:
explanation: The two terms have the same angular frequency π rad s⁻¹ but differ in phase by π/2, so they combine like perpendicular vectors. The resultant amplitude is √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √(25) = 5 cm.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Which statement correctly describes the phase relations in linear SHM?

options.A: Velocity and acceleration are in phase with each other
options.B: Displacement leads velocity by π/2 rad and velocity leads acceleration by π/2 rad
options.C: Acceleration leads displacement by π/2 rad
options.D: Velocity leads displacement by π/2 rad and acceleration leads velocity by π/2 rad

correct_answer: Velocity leads displacement by π/2 rad and acceleration leads velocity by π/2 rad
explanation: Each differentiation with respect to time advances the phase of a sinusoid by π/2. Hence velocity is ahead of displacement by π/2 and acceleration is ahead of velocity by a further π/2, making it π ahead of displacement.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: In SHM, the acceleration leads the velocity in phase by:
explanation: If x = A sin(ω t), then v = A ω sin(ω t + π/2) and a = A omega² sin(ω t + π). Subtracting the phase of v from the phase of a gives π minus π/2, which is π/2 rad.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A particle performing SHM has a speed of 4 cm s⁻¹ when its displacement is 3 cm, and a speed of 3 cm s⁻¹ when its displacement is 4 cm. The period of the motion is:
explanation: From the two conditions, 16 = omega² (A² - 9) and 9 = omega² (A² - 16). Subtracting gives 7 = omega² x 7, so ω = 1 rad s⁻¹. Substituting back gives A² = 25, that is A = 5 cm. Hence T = 2 π / 1 = 2 π s, about 6.28 s.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: For SHM of amplitude A and angular frequency ω, the speed of the particle at the mean position obtained from v = ω √(A² - x²) is:
explanation: At the mean position x = 0, so v = ω √(A² - 0) = ω A. This is the largest speed reached during the oscillation.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The necessary and sufficient condition for a particle to perform linear SHM is that:

options.A: the speed of the particle remains constant throughout the motion
options.B: the net force on it is proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is directed opposite to that displacement
options.C: the particle moves along a circular path with constant angular speed
options.D: the net force on it is constant in magnitude and always directed towards the mean position

correct_answer: the net force on it is proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is directed opposite to that displacement
explanation: SHM is defined by F = -k x with k positive. This single condition guarantees a = -omega² x, sinusoidal displacement, and a period independent of amplitude.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A particle moves along a straight line such that its acceleration is a = -k x³, where k is a positive constant and x is the displacement from a fixed point. The motion is:

options.A: oscillatory and periodic but not simple harmonic
options.C: simple harmonic with angular frequency equal to √(k)
options.D: simple harmonic with a period that depends on k alone

correct_answer: oscillatory and periodic but not simple harmonic
explanation: The acceleration is directed towards x = 0 because of the negative sign, so the particle oscillates about x = 0. However SHM demands a = -omega² x, a first power relation. Here a varies as the cube of x, so the motion is oscillatory and periodic but not simple harmonic.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: For a particle performing linear SHM, the acceleration is:

options.A: directly proportional to the square of the displacement
options.B: directly proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction to it
options.C: directly proportional to the displacement and in the same direction as it
options.D: inversely proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction to it

correct_answer: directly proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction to it
explanation: Dividing F = -k x by the mass m gives a = -(k/m) x = -omega² x. So the magnitude of acceleration grows in direct proportion to x, and its sign is always opposite to that of x.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Linear simple harmonic motion can be described as the motion of:

options.A: the projection of a uniformly accelerated straight line motion on a diameter
options.B: the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion on the tangent to the reference circle
options.C: the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion on any diameter of the reference circle
options.D: a particle moving on a circle with uniformly increasing speed

correct_answer: the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion on any diameter of the reference circle
explanation: If a reference particle moves on a circle of radius A with constant angular speed ω, its position vector makes an angle ω t + φ with a chosen axis. The foot of the perpendicular from this particle to any diameter has displacement A cos(ω t + φ), which is exactly linear SHM of amplitude A.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The SI unit of the force constant k appearing in F = -k x is:
explanation: From F = -k x, the magnitude of k is force divided by displacement. Force is measured in N and displacement in m, so k is measured in N per m, written N m⁻¹.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A body of mass 2 kg experiences a restoring force F = -8 x N, where x is in m. The period of its oscillation is:
explanation: Here k = 8 N m⁻¹ and m = 2 kg, so omega² = k/m = 8/2 = 4 and ω = 2 rad s⁻¹. Then T = 2 π / ω = 2 π / 2 = π s, which is about 3.14 s.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: As a particle performing SHM passes through the mean position, its:

options.A: speed is maximum and acceleration is zero
options.B: speed and acceleration are both maximum
options.C: speed and acceleration are both zero
options.D: speed is zero and acceleration is maximum

correct_answer: speed is maximum and acceleration is zero
explanation: Putting x = 0 gives v = ω √(A²) = A ω, the largest possible speed, and a = -omega² x = 0.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A particle performing SHM has a force constant of 200 N m⁻¹. The magnitude of the restoring force when the displacement is 0.05 m is:
explanation: Magnitude of F = k x = 200 × 0.05 = 10 N. The direction is towards the mean position.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The length of a simple pendulum whose period is 2 s is increased by 21%. The new period is:
explanation: L2/L1 = 1.21, so T2/T1 = √(1.21) = 1.1. Hence T2 = 1.1 × 2 = 2.2 s, an increase of 10% in the period for a 21% increase in length.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A simple pendulum has a period of 2 s at rest. It is now placed in a lift moving upward with an acceleration of 10 m s⁻² at a place where g = 10 m s⁻². Its new period is:
explanation: g_eff = 10 + 10 = 20 m s⁻². Hence T2 = T1 √(g/g_eff) = 2 x √(10/20) = 2 divided by √(2) = √(2) s, which is about 1.41 s.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The frequency of oscillation of a second pendulum is:
explanation: A second pendulum has a period of 2 s, so f = 1/T = 1/2 = 0.5 Hz. It completes half an oscillation every second.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI

subject: Physics
question: The length of a simple pendulum is made four times as long. Its period becomes:
explanation: Since T is proportional to √(L), multiplying L by four multiplies T by √(4) = 2. The period therefore doubles.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI

subject: Physics
question: The relation T = 2 π √(L/g) is valid only for oscillations of small angular amplitude because:

options.A: for large angles the acceleration due to gravity changes with height
options.B: only for small angles can sin(θ) be replaced by θ, which makes the restoring force proportional to the displacement
options.C: for large angles the string tension becomes zero
options.D: for large angles the mass of the bob starts to affect the period

correct_answer: only for small angles can sin(θ) be replaced by θ, which makes the restoring force proportional to the displacement
explanation: The tangential restoring force on the bob is m g sin(θ). SHM requires a force proportional to the displacement, which is satisfied only when sin(θ) can be replaced by θ, that is for small θ expressed in radian. For larger amplitudes the true period is slightly greater than 2 π √(L/g).
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The period of a second pendulum is:
explanation: A second pendulum is defined so that each one way swing takes exactly 1 s. Since one complete oscillation contains two such swings, the period is 2 s and the frequency is 0.5 Hz.

subject: Physics
question: A simple pendulum is suspended from the ceiling of a lift that moves upward with a constant acceleration a. Compared with its period when the lift is at rest, the period of the pendulum:

options.A: increases, because the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes g - a
options.B: decreases, because the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes g + a
options.C: remains the same, because the mass of the bob is unchanged
options.D: becomes zero, because the bob is pressed against the ceiling

correct_answer: decreases, because the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes g + a
explanation: In the frame of the accelerating lift a pseudo force acts downward on the bob, so the effective acceleration due to gravity is g + a. Since T is inversely proportional to √(g_eff), a larger g_eff gives a shorter period.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A second pendulum is carried to a place where the acceleration due to gravity is smaller by 2%. Its new period is nearly:
explanation: A decrease of 2% in g gives dg/g = -0.02. Then dT/T = -(1/2)(-0.02) = +0.01, an increase of 1%. Hence T = 2 × 1.01 = 2.02 s, and the pendulum clock would run slow.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Two simple pendulums of equal length carry bobs of mass 50 g and 200 g. At the same place, their periods are:

options.A: in the ratio 1 : 2, because the period varies as the square root of the mass
options.B: in the ratio 1 : 4, because the period varies directly with the mass
options.C: equal, because the period does not depend on the mass of the bob
options.D: in the ratio 2 : 1, because a heavier bob swings faster

correct_answer: equal, because the period does not depend on the mass of the bob
explanation: The restoring force is m g sin(θ) and the inertia is m, so the acceleration g sin(θ) is independent of m. The period expression therefore contains only L and g, and the two pendulums have equal periods.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: For a fixed sample of air, the graph of the speed of sound v plotted against the absolute temperature T is:

options.A: a curve that rises with decreasing steepness, while the graph of v against √(T) is a straight line through the origin
options.B: a straight line through the origin, while the graph of v against √(T) is a curve
options.C: a curve that rises with increasing steepness, while the graph of v against √(T) is also a curve
options.D: a horizontal straight line, since the speed of sound in a given gas is a constant of that gas

correct_answer: a curve that rises with decreasing steepness, while the graph of v against √(T) is a straight line through the origin
explanation: Writing the Laplace formula with the gas relation gives v = √(gamma R T / M), so v is proportional to the square root of T. A square root curve rises steeply at first and then flattens, so v against T bends over. If instead √(T) is plotted along the horizontal axis the relation becomes linear and the graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope is √(gamma R / M).
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Two diatomic gases X and Y have the same value of gamma, and the molar mass of Y is four times that of X. Gas X is at 300 K. The temperature at which the speed of sound in Y equals that in X is:
explanation: Since gamma is the same for both, equal speeds require T_X / M_X = T_Y / M_Y. With M_Y = 4 M_X this gives T_Y = 4 T_X = 4 × 300 = 1200 K. Physically, the heavier gas is four times as sluggish in molar mass, so its absolute temperature must be four times as high to give its molecules the same characteristic speed and hence the same speed of sound.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Other things being equal, the speed of sound in moist air compared with that in dry air at the same temperature and pressure is:

options.A: smaller, because the water vapour adds extra mass that the wave must set into motion
options.B: greater, because water vapour is less dense than the air it displaces
options.C: smaller, because the water droplets scatter the sound and slow it down
options.D: the same, because humidity does not enter the expression v = √(gamma P / ρ)

correct_answer: greater, because water vapour is less dense than the air it displaces
explanation: Water vapour has a molar mass of 18 g, while nitrogen has 28 g and oxygen has 32 g. When water vapour is added at fixed total pressure and temperature it displaces some of these heavier molecules, so the density of the mixture falls. Since v = √(gamma P / ρ), a smaller ρ gives a larger speed, and sound therefore travels faster on a humid day.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The pressure of a fixed mass of air is doubled while its temperature is held constant. The speed of sound in the air then:

options.A: becomes twice as large, because the speed is directly proportional to the pressure
options.B: becomes √(2) times as large, because the speed varies as the square root of the pressure
options.C: is halved, because the denser gas offers twice the inertia to the passing wave
options.D: remains unchanged, because the density doubles along with the pressure so that P / ρ is unaltered

correct_answer: remains unchanged, because the density doubles along with the pressure so that P / ρ is unaltered
explanation: Doubling the pressure of a gas at constant temperature packs the same molecules into half the volume, so the density also doubles. In v = √(gamma P / ρ) the numerator and the denominator change by the same factor, leaving the ratio and hence the speed unchanged. This is confirmed by the ideal gas relation P / ρ = R T / M, which shows that P / ρ depends only on temperature for a given gas.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Hydrogen and oxygen are both diatomic gases with the same value of gamma. At the same temperature, the molar masses being 2 g and 32 g respectively, the ratio of the speed of sound in hydrogen to that in oxygen is:
explanation: Writing P / ρ = R T / M turns the Laplace formula into v = √(gamma R T / M). With gamma and T the same for both gases, v is proportional to 1 / √(M). Hence v_H / v_O = √(M_O / M_H) = √(32 / 2) = √(16) = 4. Sound travels four times faster in hydrogen than in oxygen at the same temperature.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: In deriving his formula v = √(P / ρ) for the speed of sound in a gas, Newton assumed that the compressions and rarefactions take place:

options.A: isothermally, so that the temperature of the gas stays constant throughout the passage of the wave
options.B: at constant volume, so that the density of the gas never changes
options.C: at constant pressure, so that the elastic modulus involved is simply the atmospheric pressure
options.D: adiabatically, so that no heat enters or leaves any element of the gas

correct_answer: isothermally, so that the temperature of the gas stays constant throughout the passage of the wave
explanation: Newton argued that the heat produced in a compression would have time to flow into the neighbouring rarefaction, keeping the temperature uniform. For an isothermal change of an ideal gas the bulk modulus equals the pressure P, so his formula became v = √(P / ρ). Numerically this gives about 280 m s⁻¹ for air, some fifteen per cent below the measured value.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
subtopic: Effect of density at constant pressure
question: Two gases are kept at the same pressure and have the same value of gamma, but the density of the first is four times that of the second. The ratio of the speed of sound in the first gas to that in the second is:
explanation: With gamma and P the same for the two gases, v varies as 1 / √(ρ). If rho_1 = 4 rho_2 then v₁ / v₂ = √(rho_2 / rho_1) = √(1/4) = 1/2. The denser gas therefore carries sound at half the speed.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The Young modulus of steel is 2 × 10¹¹ N m⁻² and its density is 8000 kg m⁻³. The speed of a longitudinal wave along a long thin steel rod is:
explanation: Y / ρ = 2 × 10¹¹ / 8 × 10³ = 2.5 × 10⁷ m² s⁻². Taking the square root gives v = 5 × 10³ = 5000 m s⁻¹. Sound therefore travels through steel about fifteen times faster than through air.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The speed of sound in a given sample of air at a fixed temperature is:

options.A: greater for louder sounds of any frequency, because they carry more energy
options.B: the same for all audible frequencies, which is why a distant band is heard in tune and in time
options.C: greater for higher frequencies, which is why the shriller instruments of a distant band are heard first
options.D: greater for lower frequencies, because long wavelengths meet less resistance from the air

correct_answer: the same for all audible frequencies, which is why a distant band is heard in tune and in time
explanation: The speed of sound follows entirely from the elastic and inertial properties of the medium. Neither the frequency nor the amplitude of the disturbance appears in the expression. Hence all audible frequencies travel through the same air at the same speed, which is why a chord played at a distance still sounds as a chord.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Springs of force constants 3 N m⁻¹ and 6 N m⁻¹ are joined in series. The equivalent force constant is:
explanation: 1/k_eq = 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so k_eq = 2 N m⁻¹. Note that the series value is smaller than either individual constant, as it must be.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: Two springs of force constants k1 and k2 are connected in parallel to support the same mass. The equivalent force constant is:
explanation: Springs in parallel undergo the same extension x. The total restoring force is k1 x + k2 x = (k1 + k2) x, so the equivalent force constant is k1 + k2. A parallel combination is always stiffer than either spring alone.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: The same mass m is attached first to two identical springs of constant k in series and then to the same two springs in parallel. The ratio of the period in the series arrangement to that in the parallel arrangement is:
explanation: T_series = 2 π √(m/(k/2)) = 2 π √(2 m/k) and T_parallel = 2 π √(m/(2 k)). Their ratio is √(2 m/k) divided by √(m/(2 k)) = √(4) = 2, that is 2 : 1.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A spring mass system has a period of 2 s. The spring is cut into two equal halves and the same mass is attached to one half. The new period is:
explanation: Cutting the spring in half doubles its force constant to 2 k. Since T is inversely proportional to √(k), the new period is T divided by √(2) = 2 divided by 1.414 = √(2) s, about 1.41 s.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: In a stationary wave pattern the distance between two consecutive nodes is 20 cm and the frequency of vibration is 250 Hz. The speed of the component progressive waves is:
explanation: Since λ/2 = 20 cm, λ = 40 cm = 0.4 m. Then v = f λ = 250 × 0.4 = 100 m s⁻¹.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI

subject: Physics
question: In a stationary wave, the ratio of the amplitude of a particle situated at a distance λ/12 from a node to the amplitude of a particle at an antinode is:
explanation: With x = λ/12, k x = (2 π/λ)(λ/12) = π/6. The amplitude is 2 A sin(π/6) = 2 A x 0.5 = A, while the antinode amplitude is 2 A. The ratio is A : 2 A, that is 1 : 2.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: In a stationary wave of wavelength λ, the distance between two consecutive nodes is:
explanation: The space factor of a stationary wave is sin(k x), which vanishes whenever k x is a multiple of π. Successive zeros are separated by π/k = λ/2.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A stationary wave is represented by y = 0.1 cos(π x/6) sin(20 π t), where all quantities are in SI units. The speed of the component progressive waves is:
explanation: Here k = π/6 rad m⁻¹, so λ = 2 π/k = 12 m, and ω = 20 π rad s⁻¹, so f = 10 Hz. Hence v = f λ = 10 × 12 = 120 m s⁻¹, which is also ω/k = 20 π/(π/6).
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI

subject: Physics
question: Which statement correctly compares a progressive wave with a stationary wave?

options.A: In both waves the amplitude varies with position in exactly the same way
options.B: In a progressive wave every particle has the same amplitude, while in a stationary wave the amplitude varies with position from zero to a maximum
options.C: In both waves every particle vibrates with the same amplitude
options.D: In a progressive wave the amplitude varies with position while in a stationary wave it is the same everywhere

correct_answer: In a progressive wave every particle has the same amplitude, while in a stationary wave the amplitude varies with position from zero to a maximum
explanation: In the progressive form the coefficient of the oscillating factor is the constant A. In the stationary form the coefficient is 2 A sin(k x), which depends on where the particle is, giving zero at nodes and 2 A at antinodes.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: In a stationary wave of period T, all the particles of the medium pass simultaneously through their mean positions:

options.D: never, because the particles at the nodes are always at rest

explanation: The whole pattern becomes flat when cos(ω t) = 0, which happens at t = T/4 and t = 3T/4 in each period, that is twice in every period.

subject: Physics
question: Particles in two adjacent loops of a stationary wave:

options.B: are in phase with one another

explanation: Since sin(k x) is positive in one loop and negative in the next, the displacements of particles in adjacent loops always have opposite signs, which corresponds to a phase difference of π.

subject: Physics
question: Two waves y1 = 5 sin(4 t - 2 x) and y2 = 5 sin(4 t + 2 x), in SI units, superpose to form a stationary wave. The distance between two consecutive nodes is:

options.B: π m, that is about 3.14 m
options.C: π/2 m, that is about 1.57 m
options.D: π/4 m, that is about 0.79 m

correct_answer: π/2 m, that is about 1.57 m
explanation: Adding the two waves gives y = 10 sin(2 x) cos(4 t) apart from sign conventions. The nodes are where sin(2 x) = 0, that is 2 x = 0, π, 2 π and so on, so consecutive nodes are π/2 m apart. Equivalently λ = 2 π/2 = π m and λ/2 = π/2 m.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

subject: Physics
question: A stationary wave is given by y = 0.06 sin(π x/3) cos(100 π t), where x and y are in metre and t is in second. The distance between two consecutive nodes is:
explanation: Here k = π/3 rad m⁻¹, so λ = 2 π/k = 6 m. Consecutive nodes are separated by λ/2 = 3 m. Directly, sin(π x/3) vanishes at x = 0, 3, 6 metre and so on.

subject: Physics
question: Which of the following equations represents a stationary wave?

options.A: y = A sin(ω t + k x)
options.B: y = A sin(ω t) + A sin(k x)
options.C: y = A sin(ω t - k x)
options.D: y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(ω t)

correct_answer: y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(ω t)
explanation: Adding y1 = A sin(ω t - k x) and y2 = A sin(ω t + k x) gives y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(ω t) after using the sum to product identity. The position fixes the amplitude and the time factor is shared by all particles.

question: In the stationary wave y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(ω t), the amplitude of a particle located at a distance λ/8 from a node is:
explanation: With x = λ/8, k x = (2 π/λ)(λ/8) = π/4. Hence the amplitude is 2 A sin(π/4) = 2 A/√(2) = A √(2), about 1.41 A.

question: A wire of length 1.5 m and linear density 0.02 kg m⁻¹ vibrates in three loops when excited by a tuning fork of frequency 100 Hz. The tension in the wire is:
explanation: Three loops in 1.5 m means each loop is 0.5 m, so λ = 1 m. The wave speed is v = f λ = 100 × 1 = 100 m s⁻¹. Hence T = m v² = 0.02 × 100² = 0.02 × 10000 = 200 N.

subject: Physics
question: A sonometer wire of vibrating length L sounds its fundamental note. The pattern on the wire consists of:

options.A: one node and one antinode, with L = λ/4
options.B: two nodes at the ends and two antinodes, with L = λ
options.C: two nodes at the ends and one antinode at the middle, with L = λ/2
options.D: two antinodes at the ends and one node at the middle, with L = λ/2

correct_answer: two nodes at the ends and one antinode at the middle, with L = λ/2
explanation: Both ends are held fixed and must be nodes. The simplest pattern satisfying this has a single loop with one antinode in the middle, and one loop spans half a wavelength, so L = λ/2.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI

subject: Physics
question: A sonometer wire under constant tension is divided into three segments by two movable bridges, so that the lengths of the segments are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. The fundamental frequencies of the three segments are in the ratio:
explanation: The tension and linear density are common to all three segments, so n is proportional to 1/L. The reciprocals of 1, 2 and 3 are 1, 1/2 and 1/3, which on multiplying throughout by 6 become 6 : 3 : 2.

subject: Physics
question: A sonometer wire under a tension of 100 N sounds a fundamental note of 200 Hz. Keeping the length unchanged, the tension is increased to 225 N. The new fundamental frequency is:
explanation: The ratio of tensions is 225/100 = 2.25, whose square root is 1.5. Hence n2 = 200 × 1.5 = 300 Hz.

subject: Physics
question: A wire of length 1 m and linear density 0.01 kg m⁻¹ is to sound a fundamental note of 100 Hz. The tension required in the wire is:
explanation: The fundamental wavelength is 2L = 2 m, so v = f λ = 100 × 2 = 200 m s⁻¹. Since v = √(T/m), T = m v² = 0.01 × 200² = 0.01 × 40000 = 400 N.

subject: Physics
question: The SI unit of the quantity m that appears in the expression n = (1/2L) √(T/m) for a stretched string is:
explanation: For the expression √(T/m) to have the unit of speed, T in N divided by m must give m² s⁻². Since N is kg m s⁻², m must be in kg m⁻¹, which is indeed mass per unit length.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XI

subject: Physics
question: For a stretched string kept at constant tension and made of the same material, the fundamental frequency is:

options.B: inversely proportional to the vibrating length
options.C: inversely proportional to the square of the vibrating length
options.D: directly proportional to the vibrating length

correct_answer: inversely proportional to the vibrating length
explanation: Since n = (1/2L) √(T/m), keeping T and m fixed makes n proportional to 1/L, so the product n L stays constant.

explanation: In the fundamental mode the string carries one loop, so L = λ/2 and λ = 2L. Since v = √(T/m), the frequency is n = v/λ = (1/2L) √(T/m).

explanation: The wave speed is v = √(100/0.01) = √(10000) = 100 m s⁻¹. The fundamental frequency is n = v/(2L) = 100/(2 × 0.5) = 100 Hz.

explanation: Each loop is 1.2/4 = 0.3 m long and equals λ/2, so λ = 0.6 m. Hence v = f λ = 200 × 0.6 = 120 m s⁻¹.

explanation: Comparison with the standard form shows T = 0.01 s and λ = 3.4 m. Hence the frequency is f = 1 / T = 100 Hz and the speed is v = f λ = 100 × 3.4 = 340 m s⁻¹, the usual speed of sound in air.

question: A note of a single fixed frequency is sounded so that it travels both through air, where the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, and through water, where it is 1500 m s⁻¹. The ratio of the wavelength in air to that in water is:
explanation: The frequency is the same in both media because it is fixed by the source. Hence λ is proportional to v and lambda_air / lambda_water = 340 / 1500. Dividing both numbers by 20 gives 17 / 75. The wavelength in water is therefore several times longer than in air.

question: A sound wave passes from air into water. The quantity that certainly remains unchanged is:
explanation: The particles at the boundary are driven by the wave arriving from the air, so they vibrate at exactly the rate at which the source vibrates. question: Two points on the path of a sound wave are separated by a distance equal to one quarter of the wavelength. The phase difference between the oscillations at these two points is:
explanation: Using φ = (2 π / λ) x delta x with delta x = λ / 4 gives φ = (2 π / λ) × (λ / 4) = π / 2 rad, which is 90° or a quarter of a cycle.

question: The wavelength of a progressive wave is best defined as:

options.A: the maximum distance of a particle of the medium from its mean position
options.B: the distance travelled by the wave in one second
options.C: the distance travelled by a particle of the medium during one full oscillation
options.D: the distance travelled by the wave in the time taken by one particle of the medium to complete one full oscillation

correct_answer: the distance travelled by the wave in the time taken by one particle of the medium to complete one full oscillation
explanation: In the time T taken by a particle to complete one oscillation, the disturbance advances by a distance v T. After that time the pattern has moved forward by exactly one repeat unit, so v T is the wavelength. Writing T = 1/f gives the standard relation v = f λ.

question: In a combination of unequal capacitors,:

options.A: both the charge and the potential difference are the same for every capacitor in a series arrangement
options.B: the charge is the same on each capacitor in a series arrangement, while the potential difference is the same across each in a parallel arrangement
options.C: both the charge and the potential difference are the same for every capacitor in a parallel arrangement
options.D: the potential difference is the same across each capacitor in a series arrangement, while the charge is the same on each in a parallel arrangement

correct_answer: the charge is the same on each capacitor in a series arrangement, while the potential difference is the same across each in a parallel arrangement
explanation: In a series chain the inner plates are isolated, so induction gives every capacitor the same charge while the applied voltage divides between them. In a parallel arrangement all the capacitors are connected across the same two nodes, so they share the same potential difference while the charge divides in proportion to the capacitances.

question: A large metal slab and a large dielectric slab of dielectric constant 4 are placed separately in the same uniform electric field E, each with its plane faces perpendicular to the field. In electrostatic equilibrium, the field deep inside the metal slab and deep inside the dielectric slab are respectively:
explanation: In the metal the free electrons keep moving until the induced surface charges create a field that exactly cancels the applied field, so the internal field is zero. In the dielectric the charges are bound and can only be displaced slightly, so the bound surface charges produce a partial opposing field and the net field is reduced to E / K, here E / 4. A conductor can be regarded as the limiting case of a dielectric with an infinitely large dielectric constant.

subject: Physics

question: A solid metal sphere is given an excess charge. In electrostatic equilibrium this charge resides:

options.A: uniformly throughout the volume of the sphere
options.B: in a thin shell just inside the surface with none on the surface itself
options.C: entirely on the outer surface of the sphere
options.D: mostly at the centre of the sphere

correct_answer: entirely on the outer surface of the sphere
explanation: If any excess charge remained inside the metal, it would produce a field there and drive further motion, contradicting equilibrium. The mutual repulsion of like charges also pushes them as far apart as possible. Both arguments lead to the same conclusion: the excess charge sits entirely on the outer surface.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
source_chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
question: The essential difference between a polar and a non polar dielectric is that:

options.A: a polar dielectric contains free electrons whereas a non polar dielectric does not
options.B: a non polar dielectric cannot be polarised by an external field at all
options.C: molecules of a polar dielectric have a permanent dipole moment even with no field applied
options.D: a polar dielectric has a dielectric constant less than 1

correct_answer: molecules of a polar dielectric have a permanent dipole moment even with no field applied
explanation: In a non polar molecule such as hydrogen the centres of positive and negative charge coincide, so the molecule has no dipole moment until a field pulls the centres apart. In a polar molecule such as water the two centres are permanently separated, so a dipole moment exists even with no field. In the absence of a field these permanent dipoles point randomly, so the material shows no net polarisation until a field aligns them.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
source_chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

question: Sensitive electronic equipment is enclosed in a metal box so that external electric fields do not affect it. This use of a conducting enclosure is called:
explanation: Charges induced on the outside of the metal enclosure arrange themselves so that the field inside the cavity is zero, whatever the external field. The interior is therefore protected, and this protection is called electrostatic shielding. The same principle keeps a person safe inside a car during a lightning strike.

subject: Physics
chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
question: When a slab of dielectric is placed in an external electric field, the molecules of the dielectric:

options.A: acquire or align dipole moments, producing bound charges on the faces of the slab
options.B: move bodily towards the face of the slab nearer the positive plate
options.C: lose their charge completely and become neutral atoms
options.D: release free electrons that drift to one face of the slab

correct_answer: acquire or align dipole moments, producing bound charges on the faces of the slab
explanation: The applied field displaces the positive and negative charges within each molecule slightly, or aligns dipoles that are already present. Inside the slab the effects of neighbouring molecules cancel, but bound charges are left uncancelled on the two faces. These bound charges set up a field opposing the applied field, so the net field inside the dielectric is reduced.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
source_chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

subject: Physics
chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
question: The dielectric constant K of a medium is defined as the ratio of the field applied to a dielectric to the reduced field inside it. The dielectric constant is therefore:

options.A: a dimensionless number that is always less than 1
options.B: a quantity with the unit C² N⁻¹ m⁻²
options.C: a quantity with the unit farad per metre
options.D: a dimensionless number that is greater than or equal to 1

correct_answer: a dimensionless number that is greater than or equal to 1
explanation: K is the ratio of two quantities of the same kind, so it carries no unit and no dimensions. Because polarisation always weakens the field inside the dielectric, the reduced field is smaller than the applied one and K is at least 1, equalling 1 only for vacuum.

source_chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

question: A solid metal block is placed in an external electric field and allowed to reach electrostatic equilibrium. The electric field at every point inside the metal is then:

options.C: larger than the external field because of the induced charges
options.D: equal to the external field divided by the dielectric constant of the metal

explanation: Free electrons in the metal move under the applied field and pile up on the surfaces. Their own field opposes the applied field, and the movement continues until the two cancel exactly. Once that happens no force acts on the remaining free charges, so equilibrium is reached with zero field everywhere inside the conductor.

subject: Physics
chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
question: A neutral metal slab is placed in a uniform external electric field pointing to the right. In equilibrium the slab carries:

options.A: no charge on either face, since the slab is neutral
options.B: negative charge on its left face and equal positive charge on its right face
options.C: negative charge on both faces of the slab
options.D: positive charge on its left face and equal negative charge on its right face

correct_answer: negative charge on its left face and equal positive charge on its right face
explanation: The field pushes positive charge to the right, but only electrons are free to move, and they move to the left, against the field. The left face therefore acquires negative charge and the right face is left with an equal positive charge. These induced charges produce an internal field to the left that exactly cancels the applied field inside the metal.

chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
question: According to the principle of superposition, the electrostatic force on a point charge due to a group of other point charges is:

options.A: the vector sum of the forces due to each of the other charges taken one at a time, each force being unaffected by the presence of the remaining charges
options.B: the vector sum of the forces due to each of the other charges, each force being reduced by the screening action of the remaining charges
options.C: the force due to the nearest charge alone, since the inverse square dependence makes the others negligible
options.D: the algebraic sum of the magnitudes of the forces due to each of the other charges taken one at a time

correct_answer: the vector sum of the forces due to each of the other charges taken one at a time, each force being unaffected by the presence of the remaining charges
explanation: Coulomb's law describes a two body interaction. The force between any pair of charges is exactly the same whether or not other charges are present, and the resultant is obtained by vector addition of these pairwise forces.

question: Two identical metal spheres X and Y carry charges of 5 microC and -3 microC and are held 40 cm apart, attracting each other with a force F. A third identical uncharged sphere is touched first to X, then to Y, and is then removed far away. With X and Y still 40 cm apart, the force between them is now:
explanation: After the third sphere touches X, both carry (5 + 0) / 2 = 2.5 microC. The third sphere, now at 2.5 microC, touches Y, and the two share (2.5 - 3) / 2 = -0.25 microC each. So X finally carries 2.5 microC and Y carries -0.25 microC. The product of magnitudes changes from 5 × 3 = 15 to 2.5 × 0.25 = 0.625, a factor of 1/24. The charges are still of opposite sign, so the force is attractive and equals F / 24.

question: Two small identical balls, each of mass m and charge q, hang from a common point by insulating threads of equal length L. In equilibrium the threads make a small angle with the vertical and the balls are a distance x apart. For small angles, x varies with q as:
explanation: For each ball the horizontal Coulomb force is balanced through the thread tension: k q² / x² = m g tan θ. For small angles tan θ is approximately (x/2) / L, so k q² / x² = m g x / (2 L), giving x³ = 2 k q² L / (m g). Hence x is proportional to q²⁄³.

question: According to Coulomb's law, the magnitude of the force between two point charges at rest is:

options.A: directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the separation
options.B: directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the separation
options.C: directly proportional to the product of the charges and directly proportional to the square of the separation
options.D: directly proportional to the sum of the charges and inversely proportional to the separation

correct_answer: directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the separation
explanation: Coulomb's law states F = k q1 q2 / r². The numerator carries the product of the two charges and the denominator the square of the distance between them, so the force falls to one quarter when the separation is doubled.

question: The expression F = k q1 q2 / r² may be applied directly to two uniformly charged conducting spheres, with r taken as the distance between their centres, provided that:

options.A: the two spheres have exactly equal radii
options.B: the two spheres carry charges of the same sign
options.C: their separation is very large compared with their radii
options.D: the two spheres are made of the same metal

correct_answer: their separation is very large compared with their radii
explanation: When the spheres are close together each sphere induces a redistribution of charge on the other, so the charge is no longer uniformly distributed and the centres are no longer the effective locations of the charge. Only when the separation is much larger than the radii can each sphere be treated as a point charge at its centre.

question: Comparing Coulomb's law with Newton's law of gravitation, the correct statement is:

options.A: both vary as the inverse square of distance and both can be attractive or repulsive
options.B: only the gravitational force varies as the inverse square of distance, while the Coulomb force varies as the inverse first power
options.C: both vary as the inverse square of distance, but only the Coulomb force can be repulsive and depends on the medium
options.D: both are independent of the medium between the interacting bodies

correct_answer: both vary as the inverse square of distance, but only the Coulomb force can be repulsive and depends on the medium
explanation: Both forces act along the line joining the two bodies and both fall off as 1 / r². The differences are that charge comes in two signs so the Coulomb force can attract or repel while gravitation only attracts, that the Coulomb force is reduced by a factor K in a dielectric while gravitation is unaffected by the intervening medium, and that the Coulomb force is about 10³⁶ times stronger for two protons.

question: Two equal point charges q are fixed at the ends of a line of length r. A third charge is placed at the midpoint of this line so that the whole system is in equilibrium. That third charge must be:
explanation: Consider one of the end charges. The other end charge repels it with k q² / r² outward. The midpoint charge Q is at distance r / 2 and must attract it inward with k q |Q| / (r/2)² = 4 k q |Q| / r². Equating gives |Q| = q / 4, and the charge must be negative, so it is -q / 4. The midpoint charge is itself in equilibrium by symmetry.

question: A total charge Q is to be split into two parts q and Q - q, which are then held a fixed distance apart. The force between the two parts is greatest when q equals:
explanation: F = k q (Q - q) / r². Writing the product as q Q - q² and setting the derivative with respect to q to zero gives Q - 2 q = 0, so q = Q / 2. Equivalently, the product of two numbers with a fixed sum is largest when they are equal.

question: A charge of +1 microC and a charge of +9 microC are held a certain distance apart. Comparing the electrostatic force on the smaller charge with that on the larger charge,:

options.A: the two forces are equal in magnitude and in the same direction
options.B: the force on the smaller charge is nine times the force on the larger charge
options.C: the force on the larger charge is nine times the force on the smaller charge
options.D: the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction

correct_answer: the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
explanation: Coulomb's law gives the same expression k q1 q2 / r² for the force on each charge, because the same product of charges and the same separation appear. The forces act along the line joining the charges and point in opposite senses, forming a Newton third law pair, even though the charges and the masses may be very different.

question: Two neutral bodies X and Y are rubbed together and 6.25 × 10¹² electrons are transferred from X to Y. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the charges on X and Y are:

options.A: X carries -1 microC and Y carries +1 microC
options.B: X carries +2 microC and Y carries -1 microC
options.C: X carries +1 microC and Y carries +1 microC
options.D: X carries +1 microC and Y carries -1 microC

correct_answer: X carries +1 microC and Y carries -1 microC
explanation: Charge transferred = n e = 6.25 × 10¹² x 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ C = 1 microC. X has lost these electrons, so X is left with +1 microC, and Y which received them carries -1 microC. The algebraic total is still zero.

question: A charged body is touched to the disc of an uncharged gold leaf electroscope. The two gold leaves are seen to diverge because:

options.B: the leaves receive charges of opposite sign and attract each other
options.C: both leaves receive charge of the same sign and repel each other
options.D: the air between the leaves is heated and pushes them apart

correct_answer: both leaves receive charge of the same sign and repel each other
explanation: Charge given to the disc spreads over the whole conductor, so each leaf gets charge of the same sign. Like charges repel, so the leaves swing apart. The angle of divergence is a rough measure of the charge given.

question: Consider the two statements. Statement P: the total charge of an isolated system remains constant. Statement Q: the charge on a particle depends on how fast the particle is moving. Which is correct?

options.A: Both P and Q are true
options.B: P is false and Q is true
options.C: Both P and Q are false
options.D: P is true and Q is false

correct_answer: P is true and Q is false
explanation: Charge conservation says the algebraic total charge of an isolated system never changes, so P is true. Charge is also invariant, meaning a given particle carries the same charge whether it is at rest or moving fast, so Q is false. Mass, unlike charge, does depend on speed at relativistic speeds.

question: An ebonite rod acquires a charge of -1.6 × 10⁻⁷ C when rubbed with fur. Taking the electron mass as 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the mass of the rod:

options.A: remains exactly the same because charge has no mass

question: A positively charged rod is held close to, but not touching, an isolated neutral metal sphere. The sphere then has:

options.A: negative charge on the near face, positive charge on the far face and zero net charge
options.B: positive charge on the near face, negative charge on the far face and zero net charge

question: A glass rod rubbed with a silk cloth is found to be positively charged. During the rubbing:

options.A: protons move from the silk cloth to the glass rod
options.B: protons move from the glass rod to the silk cloth
options.C: electrons move from the silk cloth to the glass rod
options.D: electrons move from the glass rod to the silk cloth

correct_answer: electrons move from the glass rod to the silk cloth
explanation: Only the loosely bound electrons can be transferred by rubbing. The glass rod ends up positive, so it must have lost electrons, that is electrons went from the glass to the silk. The silk becomes equally negative.

question: Quantisation of charge is not evident in everyday laboratory measurements because:

options.A: charge behaves as a continuous fluid inside conductors

options.C: laboratory instruments measure current rather than charge
options.D: the elementary charge is so small that ordinary charges correspond to enormous values of n

question: A dipole of moment p is free to rotate in a uniform electric field E. Its potential energy is least, and its equilibrium is stable, when the angle between p and E is:

options.A: 0°, and this position is one of unstable equilibrium
options.B: 180°, and this position is one of stable equilibrium
options.C: 90°, and this position is one of minimum potential energy
options.D: 0°, and this position is one of stable equilibrium

correct_answer: 0°, and this position is one of stable equilibrium
explanation: U = -p E cos θ is smallest, equal to -p E, when cos θ = 1, that is θ = 0. A small displacement from this position produces a restoring torque, so the alignment with the field is stable.

question: An electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field with its axis inclined to the field. It experiences:

options.A: zero net force and zero torque in every orientation
options.B: a non zero net force and a non zero torque
options.C: a non zero net force and zero torque
options.D: zero net force and a non zero torque

correct_answer: zero net force and a non zero torque
explanation: In a uniform field the forces q E and -q E on the two charges are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel and the net force is zero. Their lines of action are different, so they constitute a couple of moment p E sin θ, which is non zero unless the dipole is aligned or antialigned with the field.

question: Which of the following is a correct property of electrostatic field lines?

options.A: Field lines start on negative charges and end on positive charges
options.B: Two field lines can never cross each other
options.C: Field lines pass continuously through the body of a conductor
options.D: Field lines always form closed loops

correct_answer: Two field lines can never cross each other
explanation: If two field lines crossed, the field at the point of crossing would have two different directions at once, which is impossible. Electrostatic lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, are never closed, and do not pass through conductors.

question: The resultant electric field at a point due to a system of point charges is obtained by:

options.A: adding the individual fields as vectors
options.B: adding the individual fields as scalars with their signs
options.C: taking the field due to the nearest charge only
options.D: adding the magnitudes of the individual fields

correct_answer: adding the individual fields as vectors
explanation: Each charge sets up its own field at the point as though the others were absent, and the resultant field is the vector sum of these contributions. Because the field is a vector, both magnitude and direction of every contribution must be taken into account.

question: In electrostatic equilibrium the electric field just outside the surface of a charged conductor is always normal to the surface because:

options.A: the conductor offers a very high resistance to charge flow along its surface
options.B: any tangential component would drive the free surface charges along the surface, so equilibrium would not have been reached
options.C: electric field lines are unable to enter any material medium
options.D: the surface charge density on a conductor is always the same at every point

correct_answer: any tangential component would drive the free surface charges along the surface, so equilibrium would not have been reached
explanation: Free charges on a conductor respond to any tangential field by moving. In the final static state there can be no such motion, so the tangential component must be zero and the field is purely normal to the surface.

explanation: In a medium the permittivity is epsilon = K ε₀, so the field becomes E' = q / (4 π K ε₀ r²) = E / K. With K = 2 the field is halved. Physically, the medium polarises and the induced bound charges partly oppose the field of the free charge.

explanation: Each charge is at a distance a / √2 from the centre, so each produces a field of magnitude k q / (a² / 2) = 2 k q / a². question: Two electric lines of force can never intersect because at the point of intersection:

options.A: the potential would have two different values
options.B: the electric field would have to be zero
options.C: the electric field would have two different directions at the same point
options.D: the charge density would become infinite

correct_answer: the electric field would have two different directions at the same point
explanation: The tangent to a line of force at any point gives the direction of the electric field there. If two lines crossed, two different tangents would exist at the crossing point, so the field would have two directions at once. Since the force on a test charge at a point is unique, this is impossible.

question: Four equal point charges, each of magnitude q and all of the same sign, are fixed at the four corners of a square. The electric field at the centre of the square is:

options.C: twice the field due to one charge, directed along a side

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
question: At a certain point a test charge of 2 microC experiences a force of 0.1 N. The test charge is then removed and replaced by a charge of -4 microC. The electric field at that point is:

options.A: 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ both before and after the replacement
options.B: 5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ both before and after the replacement
options.C: 5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ before and 2.5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ after the replacement
options.D: 5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ before and 1 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹ after the replacement

correct_answer: 5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ both before and after the replacement
explanation: E = 0.1 / (2 × 10⁻⁶) = 5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. The field at a point is created by the source charges and does not depend on the size or sign of the charge used to probe it, so it is unchanged when the test charge is replaced. Only the force on the new charge changes.

question: A hemispherical shell of radius R is placed in a uniform electric field E with its axis parallel to the field, so that the field enters through the flat circular face. The flux through the curved surface of the hemisphere is:
explanation: Treat the hemisphere plus its flat circular face as a closed surface enclosing no charge, so the total flux is zero. The flux entering through the flat face is E times its area π R². Hence the same amount, E π R², must leave through the curved surface. Equivalently, the curved surface presents a projected area π R² to the field.

question: A plane surface of area S is placed in a uniform electric field E, with θ the angle between the field and the normal to the surface. The electric flux through the surface is:

options.A: E S cos(θ), measured in N C⁻¹ m⁻²
options.B: E S tan(θ), measured in N m² C⁻¹
options.C: E S sin(θ), measured in N m² C⁻¹
options.D: E S cos(θ), measured in N m² C⁻¹

correct_answer: E S cos(θ), measured in N m² C⁻¹
explanation: Flux counts the field lines crossing the surface. Only the component of E along the normal, that is E cos(θ), contributes, so φ = E S cos(θ). The unit is newton metre squared per coulomb, equivalently volt metre.

question: A point charge q is at the centre of a spherical surface of radius R and the flux through the sphere is φ. The charge is now doubled and the radius of the sphere is also doubled. The new flux is:
explanation: Flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀ and is completely independent of the radius. Doubling the charge therefore doubles the flux, and doubling the radius changes nothing. The new flux is 2 φ. Note that the field at the surface does fall to one half, since the charge doubles while r² quadruples.

question: Electric flux is:

options.A: a scalar quantity that can be positive, negative or zero
options.B: a vector quantity directed along the electric field
options.C: a scalar quantity that can never be negative
options.D: a vector quantity directed along the normal to the surface

correct_answer: a scalar quantity that can be positive, negative or zero
explanation: Flux is defined as the scalar product of the field and the area vector, so it is a scalar. Its sign depends on the angle θ: it is positive when lines leave the surface, negative when they enter, and zero when the field lies in the plane of the surface.

question: A closed surface is drawn in a region where a strong electric field exists, but the surface encloses no net charge. The total flux through the surface is:

options.A: zero, although the field on the surface is not zero
options.B: non zero and proportional to the strength of the external field
options.C: non zero and proportional to the area of the surface
options.D: zero, and the field must also be zero everywhere on the surface

correct_answer: zero, although the field on the surface is not zero
explanation: The total flux depends only on the net charge inside. With no enclosed charge the net flux is zero. This does not make the field zero on the surface: field lines from outside charges enter on one side and leave on the other, so the incoming negative flux exactly cancels the outgoing positive flux.

subject: Physics
chapter: Electric Charges and Fields; Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
question: Which of the following describes the relation between the electric field and the electric potential correctly?

options.A: The field and the potential always vanish at exactly the same points
options.B: The field can be zero where the potential is not zero, and the potential can be zero where the field is not zero
options.C: Wherever the potential is zero the field must also be zero
options.D: Wherever the field is zero the potential must also be zero

correct_answer: The field can be zero where the potential is not zero, and the potential can be zero where the field is not zero
explanation: At the midpoint between two equal positive charges the fields cancel while the potentials add, so E = 0 and V is not zero. At the midpoint between equal and opposite charges the potentials cancel while the fields add, so V = 0 and E is not zero. The field depends on how the potential changes, not on the value the potential happens to have.

question: At a point on the equatorial line of a short electric dipole,:

options.A: both the potential and the electric field are zero
options.B: the electric field is zero while the potential is not zero
options.C: the potential is zero while the electric field is not zero
options.D: both the potential and the electric field have their largest values

correct_answer: the potential is zero while the electric field is not zero
explanation: An equatorial point is equidistant from the two charges, so the positive and negative contributions to the potential, which are scalars, cancel exactly. The field contributions are vectors: their components along the equatorial line cancel while the components parallel to the dipole axis add, giving k p / r³ antiparallel to the dipole moment.

options.A: perpendicular to the electric field lines at every point
options.B: inclined at 45° to the electric field lines
options.C: parallel to the electric field lines at every point
options.D: spherical in shape whatever the charge distribution

correct_answer: perpendicular to the electric field lines at every point
explanation: Moving a charge along an equipotential surface involves no change of potential and hence no work. Since the work equals q E times the displacement along E, the field must have no component along the surface, so it is perpendicular to the surface everywhere.

options.A: 20 N C⁻¹ directed along the positive x direction
options.B: 10 N C⁻¹ directed along the negative x direction

options.D: 20 N C⁻¹ directed along the negative x direction

explanation: dV/dx = 10 x, so E = -10 x. At x = 2 m, E = -20 N C⁻¹, that is a field of magnitude 20 N C⁻¹ pointing in the negative x direction, towards lower potential.
