syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: A pentavalent impurity atom in a silicon crystal is called a donor because:

options.A: it accepts an electron from a neighbouring silicon atom and so creates a hole
options.B: it gives up all five of its valence electrons to the conduction band at room temperature
options.C: it donates a proton to the silicon lattice
options.D: four of its valence electrons form covalent bonds and the fifth is very easily released to the crystal

correct_answer: four of its valence electrons form covalent bonds and the fifth is very easily released to the crystal
explanation: A pentavalent atom sits in a silicon site and uses four of its five valence electrons to complete the four covalent bonds. The fifth electron has no bond to join and is held only weakly by the parent atom, needing about 0.05 eV to break away. At room temperature it is released, so the atom donates a conduction electron.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: When the extra electron of a donor atom enters the conduction band, the donor atom left behind is:

options.A: a positive ion that is fixed in the lattice and cannot move
options.B: a positive ion that is free to drift towards the negative terminal
options.C: a neutral atom, since the released electron is still inside the crystal
options.D: a negative ion that is fixed in the lattice and cannot move

correct_answer: a positive ion that is fixed in the lattice and cannot move
explanation: The donor atom is covalently bonded into the lattice. When its fifth electron leaves, the atom retains its full nuclear charge but one fewer electron, so it becomes a positive ion. Being locked into the crystal it cannot contribute to conduction, but it does keep the crystal electrically neutral overall.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: Doping a semiconductor means:

options.A: adding a small controlled amount of a suitable impurity to an otherwise pure crystal
options.B: applying a strong electric field across a semiconductor crystal
options.C: removing every last trace of impurity from a semiconductor crystal
options.D: heating a pure semiconductor until its carrier concentration has doubled

correct_answer: adding a small controlled amount of a suitable impurity to an otherwise pure crystal
explanation: Doping is the deliberate addition of a tiny, carefully controlled amount of a pentavalent or trivalent element to a very pure semiconductor. Even one impurity atom in a million raises the conductivity enormously and fixes which type of carrier is in the majority.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The crystals of pure silicon and germanium are held together by:

options.A: covalent bonds, each atom sharing its four valence electrons with four neighbouring atoms
options.B: hydrogen bonds between neighbouring atoms of the lattice
options.C: ionic bonds between positive and negative ions formed by transfer of electrons
options.D: metallic bonds in which all the valence electrons form a common free pool

correct_answer: covalent bonds, each atom sharing its four valence electrons with four neighbouring atoms
explanation: Each silicon or germanium atom has four valence electrons. It shares one electron with each of four neighbours, so every atom finds itself with a stable set of eight shared electrons. All the valence electrons are locked in these bonds, which is why a pure crystal is an insulator at 0 K.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: In a semiconductor placed in an electric field, the holes move:

options.A: in the same direction as the electrons
options.B: at right angles to the applied field
options.C: in the direction of the conventional current, that is opposite to the electrons
options.D: opposite to the conventional current, alongside the electrons

correct_answer: in the direction of the conventional current, that is opposite to the electrons
explanation: The applied field pushes the positively charged hole along the field direction, which is the direction of conventional current, and pushes the negatively charged electron the opposite way. Because their charges are also opposite, the two motions give current contributions in the same sense, and they add.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The intrinsic carrier concentration of a pure semiconductor at 300 K is 2 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³. The total number of mobile charge carriers in a sample of volume 1 cm³ is:
explanation: 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³. Electrons in this volume = 2 × 10¹⁹ x 10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10¹³, and there are equally many holes. Total mobile carriers = 2 × 2 × 10¹³ = 4 × 10¹³.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: In the same semiconductor at the same temperature,:

options.A: the mobility of the holes is greater than the mobility of the electrons
options.B: the mobility of the electrons is greater than the mobility of the holes
options.C: the holes have no mobility at all, since they are not real particles
options.D: the two mobilities are exactly equal because the two concentrations are equal in a pure sample

correct_answer: the mobility of the electrons is greater than the mobility of the holes
explanation: A free electron in the conduction band moves through the crystal almost unhindered except by scattering. A hole moves only by successive jumps of bound valence electrons into the vacancy, a more sluggish process. Hence for the same field the electron drift speed is larger, and mu_e exceeds mu_h in both silicon and germanium.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: A hole in a semiconductor is:

options.A: a positively charged particle of the same mass as a proton sitting in the lattice
options.B: an empty lattice site from which a whole atom is missing
options.C: a vacancy left in a covalent bond when an electron leaves it, behaving as a carrier of positive charge
options.D: an atom of the crystal that has lost its nucleus

correct_answer: a vacancy left in a covalent bond when an electron leaves it, behaving as a carrier of positive charge
explanation: When thermal energy breaks a covalent bond the freed electron wanders through the crystal, and the incomplete bond it leaves behind is short of one electron. Relative to the neutral crystal that site carries a net positive charge of magnitude e, and because a neighbouring bonding electron can jump into it the vacancy itself moves. It is therefore treated as a mobile positive carrier.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
subtopic: Comparing n_i of Si and Ge
question: At the same temperature the intrinsic carrier concentration of germanium is about a thousand times that of silicon. This is because:

options.A: germanium atoms have more valence electrons than silicon atoms
options.B: germanium has the smaller forbidden gap, and the pair concentration depends exponentially on the gap
options.C: germanium has the larger forbidden gap, and a larger gap releases more electron hole pairs
options.D: germanium has a thousand times as many atoms per unit volume as silicon

correct_answer: germanium has the smaller forbidden gap, and the pair concentration depends exponentially on the gap
explanation: The gap of germanium is 0.7 eV against 1.1 eV for silicon, a difference of 0.4 eV. With k T about 0.026 eV at 300 K, this difference appears in an exponential factor and multiplies the carrier concentration by roughly a thousand. Hence n_i for germanium is about 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³ while for silicon it is about 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: Hole conduction in a pure semiconductor takes place because:

options.A: the positively charged lattice ions drift slowly through the crystal towards the negative terminal
options.B: the nucleus of a silicon atom migrates towards the negative terminal
options.C: the hole is a real particle that is pushed along by the field just like a free electron in vacuum
options.D: a valence electron of a neighbouring bond jumps into the vacancy, and the vacancy itself shifts the other way

correct_answer: a valence electron of a neighbouring bond jumps into the vacancy, and the vacancy itself shifts the other way
explanation: When a bond is broken the vacancy can be filled by an electron from an adjacent bond. That bond is then incomplete instead, so the vacancy has effectively moved one step in the direction opposite to the electron jump. Repeating this, the vacancy drifts along the field and behaves exactly like a mobile positive charge.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: In a pure semiconductor carrying a steady current, the electron current and the hole current:

options.A: flow in opposite directions as motions but add together as currents, because the carriers have opposite charges
options.B: are exactly equal in magnitude, because the two mobilities are equal
options.C: consist entirely of hole current, since the electrons stay bound in the lattice
options.D: flow in opposite directions and cancel each other, leaving zero net current

correct_answer: flow in opposite directions as motions but add together as currents, because the carriers have opposite charges
explanation: The field drives electrons one way and holes the other. A negative charge moving one way is equivalent to a positive charge moving the opposite way, so both motions correspond to conventional current in the same sense. The two contributions therefore add, and because mu_e exceeds mu_h the electrons carry the larger share.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The energy required to lift a valence electron into the acceptor level of a p-type crystal is:

options.A: very small, of the order of 0.01 eV to 0.05 eV
options.C: zero, because holes are present even at 0 K
options.D: equal to the full forbidden gap of the crystal

correct_answer: very small, of the order of 0.01 eV to 0.05 eV
explanation: Because the acceptor level lies only a few hundredths of an electron volt above the top of the valence band, thermal energy at room temperature is enough to move valence electrons into it. Each such transfer leaves a hole in the valence band, which is why p-type material has plenty of holes at ordinary temperatures.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: A silicon bar of length 0.1 m and area of cross section 1 × 10⁻⁴ m² has a conductivity of 2 S/m. The resistance offered between its ends is:
explanation: The resistivity is ρ = 1 / 2 = 0.5 Ω m. Then R = ρ L / A = 0.5 × 0.1 / (1 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.05 / 10⁻⁴ = 500 Ω. Equivalently R = L / (sigma A) = 0.1 / (2 × 10⁻⁴) = 500 Ω.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The electrical conductivity of a semiconductor carrying both electrons and holes is given by:
explanation: Each carrier type contributes a current density equal to its charge times its concentration times its mobility times the field. Electrons and holes carry opposite charges but drift in opposite directions, so the two current densities are in the same sense and their contributions add. This gives sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h).
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The energy level created inside the forbidden gap of silicon by a pentavalent donor impurity lies:

options.B: exactly at the centre of the forbidden gap
options.C: just below the bottom of the conduction band
options.D: just above the top of the valence band

correct_answer: just below the bottom of the conduction band
explanation: The fifth electron of a donor atom is very loosely bound, so only about 0.01 eV to 0.05 eV is needed to set it free. On the band diagram this corresponds to a level lying just below the bottom of the conduction band, so that thermal energy at room temperature ionises practically every donor.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: In a p-type semiconductor kept at room temperature the minority charge carriers are:

options.A: protons released from the nuclei of the atoms
options.B: electrons produced by the thermal breaking of covalent bonds
options.C: holes produced by the acceptor atoms

correct_answer: electrons produced by the thermal breaking of covalent bonds
explanation: Acceptor doping creates a large number of holes, so holes dominate. Thermal breaking of bonds still produces electron hole pairs, and the electrons from these pairs form the small minority population. Ionised acceptors carry a fixed negative charge but cannot move.

subject: Physics
question: A half wave rectifier feeds a 1 kohm load from a supply of peak voltage 31.4 V. Neglecting the diode resistance, the dc power delivered to the load is (take π = 3.14):
explanation: The peak current is Im = 31.4 / 1000 = 31.4 mA. Then I(dc) = 31.4 / 3.14 = 10 mA = 0.01 A. Hence P(dc) = (0.01)² x 1000 = 0.1 W. Only the dc component of the current contributes to the dc power delivered.

subject: Physics
question: A capacitor is joined across the load of a rectifier. Its purpose is:

options.A: to reduce the ripple by charging at the peaks and discharging slowly through the load
options.B: to convert alternating voltage into alternating voltage of higher value
options.C: to raise the output frequency of the rectifier
options.D: to block the dc component and pass only the ripple to the load

correct_answer: to reduce the ripple by charging at the peaks and discharging slowly through the load
explanation: During each pulse the capacitor charges to nearly the peak value. When the pulse falls away the diode stops conducting and the capacitor supplies the load, so the output voltage sags only a little before the next pulse arrives. The result is a much smaller ripple riding on a higher average voltage.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII

subject: Physics
question: In a bridge rectifier, during any one half cycle of the input:

options.A: two diodes in opposite arms conduct while the other two are reverse biased
options.B: three diodes conduct and one is reverse biased
options.D: all four diodes conduct at the same time

correct_answer: two diodes in opposite arms conduct while the other two are reverse biased
explanation: The four diodes form a ring. In one half cycle the two diodes whose arrows point away from the positive terminal and towards the load are forward biased, while the other two are reverse biased. When the input reverses, the roles swap. In both cases the current traverses the load in the same direction, giving full wave rectification without a centre tap.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII

subject: Physics
question: A full wave rectifier is fed from a 50 Hz supply. The ripple frequency at its output is:
explanation: Both halves of the input cycle are used and each produces a pulse of the same polarity through the load. Two pulses per input cycle means the output repeats twice as often, giving 2 × 50 = 100 Hz. This is one reason a full wave output is easier to smooth than a half wave output.

subject: Physics
question: The maximum theoretical rectification efficiencies of a half wave rectifier and of a full wave rectifier are respectively:
explanation: Rectification efficiency is the ratio of dc output power to ac input power. Because the full wave circuit uses both halves of every cycle, its maximum efficiency of 81.2% is exactly twice the 40.6% of the half wave circuit. These maxima are reached only when the diode forward resistance is negligible compared with the load.

subject: Physics
question: The numbers of diodes used in a half wave rectifier and in a bridge type full wave rectifier are respectively:
explanation: A half wave circuit uses a single diode which conducts during one half cycle only. A bridge circuit uses four diodes arranged so that two opposite arms conduct during each half cycle, which routes current through the load in the same direction both times. The centre tap version of the full wave circuit uses two diodes and a centre tapped transformer.

subject: Physics
question: A solar cell differs from a photodiode mainly in that a solar cell:

options.A: needs a large forward bias before it can generate a voltage
options.B: works only under a heavy reverse bias
options.C: gives out light when it is illuminated
options.D: works without any external bias and delivers electrical power to the load

correct_answer: works without any external bias and delivers electrical power to the load
explanation: Both devices generate carriers when light falls on the junction, but their purposes differ. A photodiode is reverse biased and is used to measure light, so it draws power from the supply. A solar cell has no external supply, has a large junction area to collect as much light as possible, and its photo generated carriers drive a current through the external load, so it supplies power.

question: A 6 V Zener diode carries a current of 20 mA. The power dissipated in it is:
explanation: Converting the current, I = 20 mA = 0.02 A. Then P = 6 × 0.02 = 0.12 W. The chosen diode must have a power rating comfortably above this figure, otherwise it will overheat in the breakdown region.

subject: Physics
question: A light emitting diode gives out light when it is:

options.A: unbiased and simply exposed to sunlight
options.C: forward biased, so that electrons and holes recombine near the junction

correct_answer: forward biased, so that electrons and holes recombine near the junction
explanation: Forward bias injects electrons into the p-region and holes into the n-region. When an injected electron recombines with a hole, the energy released is close to the band gap energy and in suitable materials it appears as a photon. Since injection happens only in forward bias, an LED must be forward biased to glow.

question: An LED emits red light of wavelength 620 nm. The band gap of the material used is about (take hc = 1240 eV nm):
explanation: Substituting, Eg = 1240 / 620 = 2.0 eV. Materials with a gap near 2 eV therefore emit red light. A larger gap gives shorter wavelengths, which is why blue LEDs need materials with gaps near 3 eV.

subject: Physics
question: Zener breakdown differs from avalanche breakdown in that Zener breakdown:

options.A: occurs in heavily doped junctions at low reverse voltages by direct field ionisation of covalent bonds
options.B: occurs in lightly doped junctions at high reverse voltages through collisions that multiply carriers
options.C: permanently destroys the junction every time it happens
options.D: occurs only when the junction is forward biased

correct_answer: occurs in heavily doped junctions at low reverse voltages by direct field ionisation of covalent bonds
explanation: In a heavily doped junction the depletion layer is very thin, so a reverse voltage of only a few volt produces an enormous field that tears electrons directly out of covalent bonds. That is Zener breakdown. In a lightly doped junction the layer is wide, the field is smaller, and breakdown occurs only at a higher voltage when carriers gain enough kinetic energy between collisions to create new pairs. That is avalanche breakdown.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The temperature of a reverse biased p-n junction is raised from 300 K to 350 K while the reverse voltage is kept constant. The reverse current:

options.A: falls to zero once the barrier has been crossed
options.B: decreases, because the mobility of the carriers falls as the temperature rises
options.C: stays exactly the same, because it is called a saturation current
options.D: increases markedly, because many more minority carriers are generated thermally

correct_answer: increases markedly, because many more minority carriers are generated thermally
explanation: The reverse current is limited by how fast minority carriers are produced, not by the voltage. Heating breaks many more covalent bonds, so minority carriers appear at a much greater rate on both sides of the junction. Every one that reaches the depletion layer is swept across, so the reverse current rises sharply. In silicon it roughly doubles for each 10° Celsius rise.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: A silicon junction has a barrier potential of 0.7 V across a depletion layer 0.5 micrometre wide. The force on an electron inside this layer is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C):
explanation: First the field: E = 0.7 / (0.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.4 × 10⁶ V/m. Then the force: F = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ x 1.4 × 10⁶ = 2.24 × 10⁻¹³ N. Although the number looks tiny, it is enormous compared with the force on an electron in an ordinary conductor, which is why carriers are swept across the layer almost instantly.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: In an unbiased p-n junction in equilibrium, the diffusion current and the drift current are:

options.A: unequal, giving a steady current of a few milliampere
options.B: equal in magnitude and in the same direction, giving a large steady current
options.C: equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so that the net current is zero
options.D: both exactly zero, since no carrier moves at all

correct_answer: equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so that the net current is zero
explanation: Diffusion drives majority carriers across the junction, which builds up the space charge and the barrier field. That field drives minority carriers the other way as a drift current. The barrier grows until the two currents are exactly equal and opposite, so the net current through an isolated junction is zero.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The diffusion current across an unbiased p-n junction is carried by:

options.A: the immobile donor and acceptor ions
options.B: majority carriers moving from the side where they are plentiful to the side where they are scarce
options.D: minority carriers swept across by the junction field

correct_answer: majority carriers moving from the side where they are plentiful to the side where they are scarce
explanation: There are many holes on the p-side and very few on the n-side, and many electrons on the n-side and very few on the p-side. These concentration differences drive holes to the right and electrons to the left, and both flows constitute the diffusion current, which is therefore a majority carrier current.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The barrier potentials of an unbiased silicon junction and an unbiased germanium junction are respectively about:
explanation: The barrier potential is the built-in potential difference established across the depletion layer at equilibrium. Its value depends on the material, being about 0.7 V for silicon and about 0.3 V for germanium. These are also the approximate forward voltages at which the two kinds of diode begin to conduct freely.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: A silicon junction diode of barrier potential 0.7 V is connected so that its p side is 0.3 V positive with respect to its n side. The effective height of the barrier becomes:
explanation: Making the p side positive applies a potential difference that opposes the built in barrier, so the two subtract. The effective barrier is 0.7 - 0.3 = 0.4 V. The remaining barrier is still large enough to keep the forward current small, which is why a silicon diode begins to conduct appreciably only near 0.7 V.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: A p n junction is formed by:

options.A: joining a semiconductor to a metal with a thin insulating layer between them
options.B: pressing a piece of p type material firmly against a piece of n type material
options.C: doping one region of a single semiconductor crystal with acceptors and the adjoining region with donors
options.D: doping one region of a crystal first with donors and then with an equal number of acceptors

correct_answer: doping one region of a single semiconductor crystal with acceptors and the adjoining region with donors
explanation: The two regions must belong to one single crystal, with the lattice continuing unbroken from the p side to the n side. This is achieved by diffusing or growing the two dopings into adjacent parts of the same wafer. Only then can carriers diffuse freely across the boundary and set up the depletion region.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The barrier potential of a junction diode at room temperature is about:

options.A: 7 V for silicon and 3 V for germanium
options.B: 1.1 V for silicon and 0.7 V for germanium
options.C: 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium
options.D: 0.3 V for silicon and 0.7 V for germanium

correct_answer: 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium
explanation: The built in potential difference across an unbiased junction is about 0.7 V for silicon and about 0.3 V for germanium. It is smaller than the band gap expressed in volt, and it is the voltage that a forward bias must largely cancel before appreciable current flows.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: The internal electric field in the depletion region of an unbiased p n junction is directed:

options.A: along the junction plane, parallel to the boundary between the two regions
options.B: from the n side towards the p side
options.C: outward from the middle of the depletion region towards both sides
options.D: from the p side towards the n side

correct_answer: from the n side towards the p side
explanation: The uncovered donor ions on the n side form a positive sheet and the uncovered acceptor ions on the p side form a negative sheet. The field between them runs from the positive sheet to the negative sheet, that is from the n side towards the p side, and it opposes further diffusion of majority carriers.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: Compared with its forward resistance, the reverse resistance of a junction diode is:

options.A: very much larger, typically by a factor of the order of 10⁵
options.B: very much smaller, typically by a factor of the order of 10⁵
options.C: almost the same, since the same barrier is present in both cases
options.D: exactly twice as large, since the barrier is doubled when the supply is reversed

correct_answer: very much larger, typically by a factor of the order of 10⁵
explanation: In forward bias the current for a fraction of a volt is measured in milliampere, giving a resistance of tens of Ω. In reverse bias the same or a larger voltage produces only microampere, giving a resistance of megaohm. The ratio is therefore of the order of 10⁵, and this asymmetry is what makes the diode useful.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
syllabus_reference: NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus, Unit 19: Electronic Devices

subject: Physics
question: In the depletion region of a p n junction, the layer on the p side and the layer on the n side carry respectively:

options.A: positive donor ions and negative acceptor ions
options.B: negative acceptor ions and positive donor ions
options.D: negative acceptor ions and free electrons

correct_answer: negative acceptor ions and positive donor ions
explanation: The p side was doped with acceptors, which become fixed negative ions once they have captured an electron. When the holes near the boundary diffuse away, these negative ions are left uncovered. On the n side the donors are fixed positive ions, uncovered when the electrons diffuse away. The result is a negative layer on the p side facing a positive layer on the n side.
source_document: Official NMC/NTA NEET-UG 2026 Physics syllabus; NCERT Physics, Class XII
